1:
With the great Passover behind them, the reformation turned from the sanctuary to the streets, and the witnesses read the sweeping away of the idols as the natural overflow of a people newly stirred. The reformed John Gill fixes the moment by the opening words, “when all this was finished” — the temple cleansed, the priests and Levites sanctified, the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread observed, and the seven added days of rejoicing kept. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes that timing his lesson: what had been wanting in the preparation before the feast was made up in the better thing that followed it, for when the religious exercises of a solemn ordinance are finished the hardest part of our work begins. “The comfort of communion with God,” he writes, “should kindle in us a holy zeal and indignation against sin”; if the heart has burned within us at an ordinance, that spirit of burning will consume the dross of corruption. So the worshippers went out and brake the images and cut down the groves, and would not return to their houses, long as they had been absent, till it was done — and not in Judah and Benjamin only, but in Ephraim and Manasseh, whether in cities now under Judah's protection or, Hoshea not forbidding it, in the northern land itself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the words for the idols. The “images” are maççebôth, “pillars” (compare Hosea 3:4), and the “groves” the Ashérîm, the sacred trunks emblematic of physical fertility (Hosea 4:13). That the zeal reached into Ephraim and Manasseh he explains historically: the northern kingdom was by now in the last stage of political weakness, rapidly drifting toward final ruin, so that a band of Jewish and Israelite zealots would meet no serious opposition. “Until they had utterly destroyed” he renders literally “so far as to finishing” (compare 2 Chronicles 24:10).

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses supply the politics that made such an incursion possible. Adam Clarke marvels that the reformation was carried into Israel at all, and confesses the cause uncertain — whether through a transport of religious zeal, or with the consent of Hoshea the king. John Wesley reads the destruction in Manasseh as done “by the special impulse and direction of God's spirit,” and adds that Hoshea contented himself with the worship of the calves, and did not practise the grosser idolatry of his predecessors, so that he would patiently suffer the breaking of the images of Baal and the things belonging to them. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the finished feast, Henry the zeal that communion kindles, Ellicott the pillars and sacred trees and the enfeebled north, Clarke and Wesley the royal tolerance that let the work run on into Hoshea's kingdom. Together they show a people so warmed by their recovered worship that they could not rest while the idols of their neighbours still stood.
2:
The demolition done, Hezekiah rebuilt the machinery of worship, restoring the priestly and Levitical courses that had fallen out of use. The reformed John Gill reads it as a recovery of the old order: the courses as David had fixed them, and as they had stood in the days of Jehoshaphat, but since interrupted, Hezekiah now restored and set again in their regular succession. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fill out the arrangement: he appointed the courses each according to the measure of his service (compare Numbers 7:5), the priests and Levites alike for burnt-offerings and thank-offerings, to minister, and to praise and give thanks by song and instrument in the gates of the camp of Jahve — that is, in the temple and the court of the priests (see 1 Chronicles 9:18).

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, traces the system back to its author: Hezekiah restored the rotation of service ascribed to David, the very order invoked at 2 Chronicles 8:14, “according to the order of David.” The phrase “every man according to his service” he renders literally “after the mouth,” that is the rule or prescription, of his service, the same idiom as Numbers 7:5; and “to minister... and praise” he calls the chronicler's usual definition of the Levitical functions. The closing words “in the gates of the tents of the LORD” he reads literally “in the gates of the camps of Jehovah,” explained at 1 Chronicles 9:18-19.

Over that word “tents” the wesleyan-arminian witnesses linger. Adam Clarke reads “the gates of the tents of the LORD” simply of the temple, “for this was the house, tabernacle, tent, and camp, of the Most High.” John Wesley draws out why so settled a house should still be called by so movable a name: within the gates of the house of the Lord, called tents “because the host of the Lord, the priests and Levites, encamped there” — and perhaps, he adds, to intimate that it was shortly to be removed. The witnesses do not contend. Gill and Ellicott fix the Davidic pattern recovered, Keil the twofold service of sacrifice and song, Clarke and Wesley the meaning of the “tents” in which that service was kept. Together they show a reformation that did not improvise a new worship but recalled the temple to its ancient and appointed method, so that every man again knew his place, his time, and his work; for, as the whole passage teaches, good order contributes much to the carrying on of a good work.
3:
The king's next act was to endow the altar from his own purse, and the witnesses weigh both the generosity and the law behind it. The reformed John Gill notes that the portion came out of Hezekiah's own treasury, a royal bounty over and above what kings usually gave for their private sacrifices, the more needful because the temple treasury was exhausted and the people brought low in the last reign. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch are precise about what was given: the material for the burnt-offerings commanded in Numbers 28 and 29 — the morning and evening offerings, and those of the sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts — the king supplied from his possessions, the substance afterward enumerated at 2 Chronicles 32:27-29.

Charles Ellicott renders the clause carefully: “the king's portion,” that is the part he contributed from his property, went for the burnt-offerings of the morning and the evening, and those on the sabbath, the new moons, and the set feasts. The victims prescribed in Numbers 28 and 29 the king furnished out of his own revenues; and the “set feasts” he identifies as the three great festivals enumerated in the law. Both grammatical-historical witnesses thus fasten the king's liberality to the statute: he did not invent offerings but paid, from his own estate, for the standing sacrifices the law already required.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the motive of the gift. Adam Clarke conjectures that the Jewish kings, at least from David's day, had furnished the daily morning and evening sacrifice at their own charge, and several others besides; so Hezekiah did but resume an old royal duty. John Wesley sharpens the tenderness in it: the cost had hitherto been drawn from the treasures of the temple, but that he might ease the people in the poverty his predecessor had brought upon them, and engage them to a more cheerful attendance on God's service, the king took the burden upon himself. It was, the whole account implies, a generous act of piety in which he consulted at once God's honour and his people's ease, a faithful servant to the one and a tender father to the others. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the exhausted treasury that made the gift needful, Keil and Ellicott the lawful offerings it purchased and the wealth it flowed from, Clarke the ancient royal custom it revived, Wesley the mercy toward an impoverished people that moved it. Together they show a prince who would rather spend from his own than see the altar fail or his subjects burdened.
4:
Having given from his own, the king next required his subjects to render what the law had long assigned, that the ministers might be free for their work. The reformed John Gill reads the “portion of the priests and the Levites” as what was appointed them by God's law — the tithes, the firstfruits, and the like. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch spell out that maintenance: the priests and Levites lived from the firstfruits (Exodus 23:19; Numbers 18:12; Deuteronomy 26:2) and the tithes the people paid from cattle and field (Leviticus 27:30-33; Numbers 18:21-24). Hezekiah commanded the inhabitants of Jerusalem to render this portion, “that they might be encouraged in the law of the LORD” — which Keil reads as “that they might hold themselves firmly to the law,” devoting themselves to their appointed duties without being forced to labour for their own subsistence, the very lack lamented at Nehemiah 13:10.

Charles Ellicott renders the command “And he said to the people,” to wit the dwellers in Jerusalem, and traces the portion to the same body of law — the firstfruits and tithes of Exodus 23:19, Leviticus 27:30-33, and Numbers 18:12. The phrase “that they might be encouraged in the law” he corrects to “that they might stick fast unto the law,” noting that the verb châzaq bears the physical sense of a thing lodged fast, as at 2 Samuel 18:9, where Absalom's “head stuck fast in the terebinth.” The meaning, he says, is that the ministers might give themselves wholly and solely to their religious duties, undistracted by any secular anxiety, and he too points to the fled and scattered Levites of Nehemiah 13:10.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads “encouraged” to the same end: the portion freed them from worldly cares and distractions, and enabled them to give up themselves entirely to the serious study of God's law, and to the instruction, direction, and quickening of the people. So the witnesses converge on a single purpose beneath the command. The tithe was not a mere due to be collected but the means of a settled and studious ministry; for a scandalous maintenance makes a scandalous ministry, and Hezekiah, having himself been liberal, could with a good grace require his subjects to be just to the temple service. Gill fixes the lawful dues, Keil and Ellicott the body of statute behind them and the sense of “sticking fast” to the law, Wesley the freedom for study and teaching that the portion secured. Together they show a reformation that understood ministers must be not merely maintained but so provided that they could attend the law of God without an eye to their own fields.
5:
The command met a ready obedience, and the people poured in the firstfruits of corn, wine, oil, honey, and every increase of the field, and the tithe of all things abundantly. The reformed John Gill observes that the commandment was not only published in Jerusalem but its report spread throughout the cities of Judah, and was answered on every hand. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that when the royal word went forth the Israelites brought in abundance the firstfruits assigned to the priests and the tithes paid to the whole tribe of Levi (Numbers 18:21-24). Over the surprising phrase “the tithe of holy things” they pause: since the law (Numbers 18:8) speaks not of a tenth of the consecrated gifts but of heave-offerings, Bertheau, they report, could find no exact correspondence between the statute and the practice here described.

Charles Ellicott renders the opening “when the word broke forth,” that is spread abroad, and takes “the children of Israel” here for the people of Jerusalem, who in the chronicler's own day had a pre-eminent right to the name; the firstfruits, he notes, were for the priests (Numbers 18:12), the tithe for the Levites (Numbers 18:21-24). So the two grammatical witnesses read the givers a little differently — Keil of the Israelites at large, Ellicott of the Jerusalemites first — but agree that firstfruits and tithe alike came in without stint.

A genuine, if small, difference opens over the “honey.” The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the plain sense: honey, though it might not be burnt upon the altar (Leviticus 2:11), could yet be offered to the priests as firstfruits or in the way of tithes, so that the people brought the tenth of all their produce whether commanded or not. John Wesley demurs, reading the word rather of “dates,” as the Hebrew writers generally understand it, sweet as honey and given because the law requires tithes only of the fruits of trees, of the earth, or of beasts. Wesley also marks the widening of the command: it came “abroad” when the king extended to all his kingdom what verse 4 had confined to Jerusalem. The witnesses do not divide over the abundance, only over a word and the givers' precise identity. Gill fixes the report spreading through Judah, Keil and Ellicott the lawful firstfruits and tithe and the puzzle of “holy things,” Clarke and Wesley the honey or the dates. Together they show a people who needed only to be asked, answering the recovered law with a flood of offerings.
6:
The country followed the capital, and the men of Israel and Judah in the outlying cities brought the tithe of oxen and sheep and of the holy things, and laid all by in heaps. The reformed John Gill sees no need of the supplied word “concerning”: the sense is simply that when the king's edict was known in the country towns as at Jerusalem, the inhabitants there too paid in their dues. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott distinguishes the parties: “the children of Israel and Judah that dwelt in the cities of Judah” are those who had left the northern kingdom to settle in the south (compare 2 Chronicles 10:17; 2 Chronicles 11:16; 2 Chronicles 30:25), set over against “the children of Israel” who dwelt in Jerusalem in the verse before.

Over “the tithe of holy things” Ellicott labours honestly at a hard phrase. It is assumed, he says, to be equivalent to “the heave-offerings of the holy things” (Numbers 18:19) — those portions of the sacrificial gifts not consumed on the altar — for “tithe of things consecrated,” taken literally, would be a surprising and wholly isolated expression. He records that the Septuagint, by an old copyist's slip, read “tithes of goats” (aigôn for agiôn), while the Vulgate follows the Hebrew; and he suspects a lacuna in the text. The closing clause “laid them by heaps” he renders literally “made heaps heaps,” that is many heaps, matching the Vulgate's “many heaps.”

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, carry the account forward: the heaps were begun in the third month and finished in the seventh, framed by Pentecost at the one end and the feast of tabernacles at the other. And the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains the very existence of the heaps: what the priests and the Levites had occasion for they made use of, “and the overplus was laid in heaps” — so that the piles were not hoarded surplus but the visible remainder after a well-supplied ministry had taken its need. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the country's obedience, Ellicott the northern settlers who shared it and the crux of “holy things,” Keil the harvest months that filled the heaps, Wesley the overplus of which they were built. Together they show the tithe rising into visible mounds in the courts of the temple, a standing witness that the law, once honoured, could feed its ministers many times over.
7:
The verse dates the piling of the heaps between two feasts, and the witnesses read the calendar as the frame of the whole harvest. The reformed John Gill names the third month Sivan, in which fell the feast of Pentecost, called the feast of harvest, when the barley harvest was ended and the wheat harvest began and the firstfruits were brought — the natural moment for the heaps to be founded. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, following the Targum, gives both months their names: the third Sivan, the seventh Tisri; and he explains the heaps as the vast collections of grain the tithes yielded over and above the ministers' own consumption, as the tenth verse will confirm.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the same seasons with a philologist's eye. The third month, Sivan, answering to our May and June, was the end of wheat-harvest, when Pentecost — the Feast of Harvest or of Firstfruits — was kept. The phrase “to lay the foundation” he traces to a curious form, lîsôd, met with only here (comparing the like form at Isaiah 51:16). The seventh month, Tisri, answering to September and October, was the time of the great Feast of Tabernacles, held after all the fruits had been gathered in and the vintage was over. So the heaps grew across the whole ingathering, from the first sheaves to the last clusters.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the two months together into a single agricultural arc: the third month of the sacred year, in which their harvest began, and the seventh, in which their harvest ended and the feast of tabernacles was kept. The witnesses do not divide; they agree, almost to a voice, on the plain meaning — that the offerings were founded when the grain first came in and completed when the last fruit was stored. Yet the very agreement carries a quiet lesson the passage means the reader to feel: all harvest-time the heaps were increasing, for God was to have his dues out of every crop as it was gathered, and only when the harvest wholly ended were the heaps finished. Gill and Clarke and Wesley fix the two feasts that bounded the work, Ellicott the rare word for its founding and the seasons behind the names. Together they show a people whose giving kept exact pace with God's giving, the mounds of tithe rising through four months of harvest until the granaries of the temple were full.
8:
When the king and his princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the LORD and his people Israel — and the witnesses find in that double blessing the fitting response to a work of grace. The reformed John Gill notes plainly that what they saw were the heaps of the tithes and firstfruits, grown to a height that called for praise. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the blessing as unfeigned thanksgiving: when Hezekiah and the leaders saw these heaps they praised the Lord and his people Israel, and the historian passes at once to the king's inquiry after their cause.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley parts the blessing into its two objects, and shows the fitness of each. They “blessed the LORD” both for giving such plentiful provisions to his land and for giving his people such liberal hearts; and “his people Israel” they blessed — that is, they praised the people for their forwardness and faithfulness in bringing the offerings in. The one act of the mouth thus rendered thanks upward to the Giver and commendation outward to the givers, acknowledging that both the harvest and the heart to part with it had come from God. And in blessing “his people Israel,” the leaders spread their approval over the whole company that had answered the call — the men of Judah and the northern settlers alike, whose faithfulness in bringing the offerings in was the very thing they praised.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the graciousness of that commendation. The king and princes gave thanks to God for his good providence, which gave the people something to bring, and for his good grace, which gave them hearts to bring it; and they blessed the people, that is, commended them for their present well-doing “without reproaching them for their former neglects.” It is observable, Henry adds, that having tasted the sweetness of God's ordinance in the late passover, they were now free in maintaining the temple service; for those who experience the benefit of a settled ministry will not grudge the expense of it. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the heaps that drew the blessing, Keil the praise that met them, Wesley the twofold thanks to God and to the people, Henry the grace of a commendation that overlooked past failings. Together they show leaders who could look on a mountain of offerings and see, not their own success in raising it, but the double gift of God — the plenty in the land, and the willing heart in the people that brought it home.
9:
The king's blessing turned to a question, and the witnesses read Hezekiah's inquiry after the heaps as prompted less by suspicion than by wonder. The reformed John Gill offers two possibilities: he asked how they came to be so large, or why the priests let them lie where they did. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch settle the point: the king questioned the priests and Levites concerning the heaps, not to learn whether they were sufficient for the ministers' support, but to learn how it happened that such masses had been piled up at all — an abundance that itself demanded explanation.

Charles Ellicott confirms the sense from the grammar. “Hezekiah questioned with the priests and the Levites” he renders “Hezekiah asked the priests,” the construction being dârash ‘al, as at 2 Samuel 11:3 and 1 Samuel 28:7; and the king's wish, he agrees, was to know how it was that the heaps of offerings had grown so large. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it in the same key: the king questioned how it came to pass that no more of their provision was spent, and that there yet remained such great heaps of it — the surprise being not scarcity but surplus.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very direction of the question is instructive. A king reforming a long-neglected worship might have feared the offerings would fall short; Hezekiah's problem is the opposite, and his inquiry betrays a mind still marvelling that obedience had produced such plenty. There is no hint that he suspected the priests of hoarding for themselves; the heaps were the honest overplus of a well-fed ministry, and the king wished only to understand the wonder before him. Gill weighs the two things he might have asked, Keil fixes that he asked not after sufficiency but after cause, Ellicott the idiom of the asking, Wesley the astonishment that so much should be left when so much had been used. Together they show the reformation reaching a moment its architects had scarcely dared expect — a temple so richly supplied that its own king had to ask how the abundance came to be. It is a happy embarrassment, and one the reformers had hoped for without daring to presume: not how to eke out a scanty provision, but how to house an overflowing one — a question the high priest will answer in the verse that follows with a single word, that the LORD hath blessed his people.
10:
Azariah the chief priest gave the answer, and it was a doxology: since the people began to bring the offerings into the house of the LORD, we have had enough to eat and have left plenty, for the LORD hath blessed his people. The reformed John Gill identifies the speaker as the high priest of the family of Eleazar, in the line of Zadok whom Solomon had raised when Abiathar was thrust out, and notes that Jarchi takes him for the same Azariah who withstood king Uzziah. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott thinks him possibly that very Azariah of 2 Chronicles 26:17, but Keil and Delitzsch judge it “hardly” the same man, who forty years before had tried to bar Uzziah from the holy place — so a real question hangs over the priest's identity, whether this is the aged opposer of Uzziah or another of his honoured name.

On the words of his reply the grammatical witnesses are exact. Ellicott renders the animated Hebrew “eating and being satisfied, and leaving over, even unto abundance” — a string of exclamatory infinitives like those of Hosea 4:2 — and reads the closing “this great store” as an accusative better taken “and there is left this great store.” The chambers the king would prepare he identifies as the temple cells, léshâkôth (compare 1 Chronicles 9:26), probably needing only clearance and cleansing to receive the stores.

What the priests did not mean by their answer, the whole passage is careful to say. They did not hoard the heaps from covetousness, but kept them to show what plentiful provision God's law had made for his ministers, could it but be gathered in; and to testify that those who give God his dues bring a blessing on all they have. “Since they began to bring in the offerings, the LORD hath blessed his people” — the very promise of Malachi 3:10, that upon the tithe brought into the storehouse God would pour out a blessing there should not be room to receive, and of the returning harvests of Haggai 2:19. The witnesses do not divide over the doxology, only over the man who spoke it. Gill and Ellicott lean toward the Azariah of Uzziah's day, Keil away from him; all agree the answer traced the heaps to a single source. Together they show a high priest who, asked to explain a mountain of provision, would not take the credit to the people's diligence nor to his own economy, but laid it wholly at the door of God, who blesses those who bring him his own.
11:
Moved by the answer, Hezekiah gave order for the offerings to be safely stored, and the witnesses read the preparing of the chambers as the wisdom that would preserve what zeal had gathered. The reformed John Gill notes the command was either to build new chambers or to fit up those already standing, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it simply as making granaries to lay up the superabundance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch leave the point open — the verb hekîn may mean either to build or to make ready — and pass to the use: into these cells the ministers brought the firstfruits, the tithes, and the dedicated things “with fidelity” (compare 2 Chronicles 19:9), under the oversight of Cononiah the Levite and Shimei his brother.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the storing a study in prudent stewardship. Hezekiah provided that the holy things should be carefully laid up, and not left in loose heaps exposed to waste and embezzlement; so he ordered chambers made ready in the courts of the temple, and the offerings brought in and kept under lock and key. “This wisdom of laying up the surplus in days of plenty,” Henry writes, “we may learn from the ant, who provideth meat in summer” (as Proverbs 6:8 commends). Nor was the care merely defensive: the very laying-up of what was brought in was itself an encouragement to the people to pay in their contributions, “for that will be given cheerfully by the public which appears to be well husbanded.”

So the witnesses gather around a single practical virtue. The offerings that grace had multiplied might yet be lost through carelessness, and Hezekiah would not have a reformation undone by neglect; he built store-chambers as carefully as he had restored the courses. Gill and Clarke fix the making of the granaries, Keil the fidelity with which the stores were brought in and the officers set over them, Henry the double wisdom of it — that hoarded plenty be guarded like the ant's summer store, and that visible good husbandry itself invites further giving. Together they show that the reformation was not content to stir a burst of generosity but took pains to keep it, providing that what the people gave to God should be neither wasted nor embezzled but held in trust for the very service it was meant to sustain. The naming of the faithful keepers, in the verses that follow, is the fruit of this same forethought.
12:
The stores were brought in faithfully, and the witnesses fasten on that word “faithfully” and on the officers set to guard the trust. The reformed John Gill reads it of the ministers' integrity: they kept nothing back for their own private use, but faithfully delivered in and laid up the whole that was brought and remained. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott parses the deposit: “the offerings” are the Terûmah or heave-offering (here the firstfruits), the tithe, and the holy things; “faithfully” is “with faithfulness” or honesty, the same word as at 2 Chronicles 19:9. Over the storehouse Cononiah the Levite was ruler, and Shimei his brother “the next,” that is second in charge; the name Cononiah, Ellicott notes, is properly Kânanyâhû, “Iahu hath established.”

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, set out the chain of oversight that these verses establish: Cononiah as ruler and Shimei his brother as second, and beneath them the ten Levites named in the next verse as overseers, the whole ordered “at the command” of the king — ex mandato Hizkiae — with Azariah the prince of the house of God, the high priest of the tenth verse, at the head of all. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds only the small clarifying note that Shimei “was the next,” being assistant to Cononiah.

Brief as the notice is, the witnesses let its point stand: that a treasure gathered by grace was committed to men chosen for their trustworthiness, and handled with a fidelity worthy of the gifts. The reformation did not merely amass offerings; it named responsible keepers and bound them to honesty, so that what was consecrated to God should be administered as before God. Gill fixes the ministers' self-denial in keeping nothing back, Ellicott the exact contents of the deposit and the meaning of the chief keeper's name, Keil the ordered ranks of oversight under the king and the high priest, Clarke the place of Shimei as second. Together they show the offerings passing into safe and faithful hands — the firstfruits, the tithe, and the dedicated things laid up under named and answerable officers, that the abundance which the LORD had blessed his people to bring might be kept as scrupulously as it had been given. The care may seem excessive for a store of grain and oil, but the witnesses feel its fitness: gifts laid up for God are not common property, and the men who handle them stand answerable to him for every measure. Fidelity, not abundance, is the note the verse strikes.
13:
A roll of ten Levitical overseers follows, and the witnesses attend to their place in a careful chain of command. The reformed John Gill reads them as assistants to the two chief keepers: these ten were under Cononiah and Shimei, at their command, ready at hand to do whatever they should order and direct. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses that nothing is known of the ten, though some of the names recur elsewhere — Jehiel and Mahath among the Levites of 2 Chronicles 29:12. “Under the hand of Cononiah” he renders “at the side of,” meaning under his orders; and he marks an unusual usage in “at the commandment of Hezekiah,” for the word miphqâd ordinarily denotes a census, as at 1 Chronicles 21:5, though the Septuagint rightly took it here of the king's command. Azariah he calls the nâgîd, the ruler, of the house of God (compare 1 Chronicles 9:11), named already in the tenth verse.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, complete the hierarchy the verse implies: to the two chief officers were subordinated these ten named Levites as under-overseers, the whole appointed by the king and by Azariah the prince of the house of God — so that the administration ran in an orderly descent from throne and high priest, through the two rulers, to the ten who did the daily work.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the reason such men were needed. Church treasures, he says, are not to be hoarded but faithfully laid out; and so officers were appointed, men of approved wisdom and faithfulness, both to keep the stores and to distribute them, that no part should be wasted, embezzled, or unjustly withheld. Treasurers were set over the offerings “to see that moth and rust did not corrupt them, nor thieves break through to steal” — the very perils of Matthew 6:20. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the ten as ready assistants, Ellicott the obscurity of their names and the idioms that govern them, Keil the ordered descent of authority, Henry the wisdom and fidelity their office required. Together they show a treasury governed not by one man's hand but by a graded company of trusted keepers, so that the wealth the people had consecrated should be administered openly and honestly, under the eye of king and high priest alike — that no single hand could waste or divert what a whole nation had given.
14:
From storing the offerings the account turns to distributing them, and names Kore the porter of the east gate, set over the freewill offerings. The reformed John Gill places him at the east gate of the temple. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the post from 1 Chronicles 9:18, and defines the charge: Kore had oversight of “the freewill offerings of God,” the voluntary gifts of Deuteronomy 12:17, and his duty was to give out “the oblations of the LORD and the most holy things” to the priests. The “oblations” he explains as the Terûmah of Jehovah, the portion of the offerings which, though consecrated to God, was transferred by him to the priests (Leviticus 7:14, 32); and “the most holy things” as that part of the sin and trespass offerings (Leviticus 6:10) and of the meat offerings (Leviticus 2:3) which the priests were to eat within the sanctuary.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, set Kore at the head of a distributing staff: under his hand were six Levites, named in the next verse, stationed in the priests' cities, whose task was to give to their brethren by their courses, “as well to the great as to the small” — that is, to the older and the younger alike. By “the brethren in their courses” they understand not only the Levites resident in the priests' cities who by youth or age could not come to the temple, but also those who at any time were off duty, since the courses served by turns.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads “the most holy things” as the remainders of the freewill offering, the sin-offering, the trespass-offering, and the shewbread, distributed so that all the ministers should have a competent maintenance for themselves and their families. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes Kore's station at the east gate, Ellicott the exact nature of the oblations and most holy things he dispensed, Keil the staff beneath him and the brethren, great and small, they were to supply, Wesley the sacred remainders that made up the ministers' portion. Together they show the second half of the system now in view: the offerings, safely stored under Cononiah, were now to be justly parted out through Kore and his six, so that every priest and Levite, in the temple or in the country towns, on duty or at rest, old or young, should receive his due share of what the people had brought.
15:
Six Levites are named as Kore's deputies, charged to distribute to the priests in their several cities. The reformed John Gill explains the division of labour: Kore was the principal, and his business lay chiefly with the priests in the temple and in Jerusalem, while these six men under him were employed in distributing to the priests scattered through the country towns. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders “next him” as “by his hand” (‘al yâdô, compare 1 Chronicles 25:2), meaning subordinate to him; the six were stationed in the sacerdotal cities to deal out a fair share of the firstfruits, tithes, and dedicated things to their brethren there. The phrase “in their set office” he prefers to attach to the following verb — “honestly to give” — rendering the Hebrew be'emûnah “in trust” or “in good faith,” and “brethren by courses” he reads “the brethren in the courses,” those of the Levitical classes not then on duty at the temple, dwelling in their towns, with the great and small taken as older and younger.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads their commission to the same effect: these were intrusted with receiving and distributing the several portions belonging to the priests who abode in their own cities, while their brethren went up in turn to serve at Jerusalem. So the resident and the absent, the serving and the waiting, were alike provided for by a settled and equitable hand.

Adam Clarke, also of the wesleyan-arminian school, pauses over a name. For “Miniamin” several of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts read “Benjamin,” and this is the reading of the Vulgate, the Syriac, the Septuagint, and the Arabic — a small textual variant that leaves the man's identity, though not his office, in doubt. The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Gill fixes the six as country deputies under Kore, Ellicott the subordination and the honest, faithful distribution to the off-duty brethren, Wesley the care for priests resident while others served, Clarke the variant in the second name. Together they show the distribution reaching down to the smallest and remotest — a fair portion carried, through named and trusted officers, to every priest in every priestly city, whether he stood that week at the altar or waited his turn at home. It is the same evenhandedness the whole chapter presses: that the serving and the resting, the near and the far, should each receive by rule and not by favour, so that none of God's ministers, however obscure his station, should be forgotten in the sharing.
16:
The distribution extended beyond the ministers to their households, and the verse begins the register that governed it — the males from three years old and upward who entered the house of the LORD. The reformed John Gill explains the office and the age together: the officers were to give not only to the priests but to the males in their genealogy, three years old and upward. Under that age, he reports from Kimchi, a child was not fit to come into the temple, having no knowledge to keep what was put into his hands, nor fitness to handle the offerings lest he defile them; but at three he might be taught to hold them and grow used to the service. Females, Kimchi adds, were not admitted at any age.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch and Charles Ellicott alike read the verse as a parenthesis marking an exception. Ellicott renders it: “apart from their register of males from three years old and upward” — the register, that is, of all who came into the house of Jehovah for the daily portion (“for a day's matter in its day,” compare 2 Chronicles 8:13 and Nehemiah 11:23) for their service in their offices by their divisions. The meaning, he explains, is that the Levites on duty in the temple, and their male children of three years and upward registered with them, were not provided for by Kore's officers, because they received their daily portion in the sanctuary itself; and children, it appears, were allowed to accompany their fathers to the temple and eat with them of the sacrifices.

So the witnesses converge on a careful distinction the verse is drawing: between the ministers serving at Jerusalem, fed on the spot from the daily portion, and their brethren in the country towns, supplied by Kore's deputies from the stores. Gill fixes the age of three and the reasons behind it, and the exclusion of the females; Keil and Ellicott the parenthetic force of the notice and the register of temple servers fed in the sanctuary. Together they show a provision reaching even to the little ones — the small sons of the priests, brought at three years old into the courts to eat of the holy things beside their fathers — and an administration so exact that it distinguished, in its very bookkeeping, those maintained at the temple from those maintained in the field, that neither company might be forgotten and neither be served twice over.
17:
The register is described further — the priests enrolled by their fathers' houses, and the Levites from twenty years old and upward in their charges by their courses. The reformed John Gill reads it plainly: as the priests were registered according to their families from the age already noted, a portion was given them, and so likewise to the Levites. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls the verse a parenthesis on the registration, prompted by the word “register” in the verse before, and translates: “as to the register of the priests, it was according to their clans” — their fathers' houses — “and the Levites from twenty years old and upward were in their offices in their divisions,” citing for the age of service 1 Chronicles 23:24.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, treat the verse as an elucidating remark upon the catalogues: the priests reckoned after the fathers'-houses, and the Levites entered upon their service at twenty years, all their duties being discharged by the several courses in rotation — and they too point to David's numbering of the Levites from twenty, at 1 Chronicles 23:27. The twenty-year threshold is worth a moment's notice, for the older law of the wilderness had set the Levite's service later; David, in his last days, had lowered the age to twenty when the ark had rest and the burdens of the tabernacle ceased, and it is that later reckoning the chronicler here assumes.

The witnesses do not divide; the verse is technical, and they read it as one. Gill fixes the two registers, of priests by family and Levites by age; Ellicott and Keil the parenthetic force of the notice and the Davidic rule of service from twenty years. Yet the dry enrolment carries the passage's steady concern: that the distribution should be governed not by favour or guesswork but by an exact roll, so that every priestly clan and every Levite of serviceable age had a known and recorded claim upon the stores. The reformation that had gathered the offerings and stored them under faithful keepers now saw to it that they were parted out by register, each man receiving according to his house and his course. Together the witnesses show a ministry provided for by rule, its very genealogies pressed into the service of a fair and orderly maintenance; the register that had once merely proved a man's descent now secured his daily bread.
18:
The register widened to embrace the whole household — the little ones, the wives, the sons and daughters of the ministers, throughout all the congregation — and the witnesses read in the closing clause a word of quiet devotion. The reformed John Gill notes that all were genealogized and registered, wives and children, sons and daughters, small or grown, and a portion distributed to each according to their number. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, taking up the thread broken off at the fifteenth verse, reads the six Levites as charged to give to their brethren, and further to keep the register of “all their little ones, their wives and their sons and their daughters, of the whole corporation” of priests — the board of Levites maintaining a roll of all who had a claim on the provisions they distributed; “through all the congregation” he renders “to a whole assembly” of the ministers' wives and children.

Over the last words, “in their set office they sanctified themselves in holiness,” a real difference of reading opens. Ellicott offers, first, that be'emûnah means “in trust” or “faithfulness” (compare 1 Chronicles 9:22), and “they sanctified themselves” that they “used to show themselves holy” — behaved conscientiously — in regard to the hallowed gifts they had to distribute; though he grants the Authorised Version may be substantially right, that the Levites simply fulfilled their trust in perfect good faith. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, following bishop Patrick, reads it otherwise and inwardly: “in faith they sanctified themselves” — the priests attended their ministry at the house of God “not doubting but they should be provided with all things necessary,” and because they served God in that confidence, care was taken that they should not be made ashamed of their hope.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the clause as the reason the households were fed from the holy things at all: their wives and children were provided for out of the sacred gifts “because they sequestered themselves from worldly affairs,” by which they might otherwise have provided for their families. So a genuine question remains — whether the ministers “sanctified themselves” by handling the holy things conscientiously, or by trusting in faith that God would provide — with Ellicott inclining to the former and Henry to the latter. But the witnesses do not divide over the mercy of the arrangement. Gill fixes the whole household enrolled, Ellicott the register of every claimant, Henry the faith that dared to serve trusting provision, Wesley the sequestration from worldly business that made provision just. Together they show a maintenance stretched to cover not the ministers only but their wives and their smallest children, that a man set apart wholly for God need not watch his family go unfed.
19:
The care reached out at last to the priests scattered on the pasture-lands of their cities, and named officers to supply them too. The reformed John Gill explains that the sons of Aaron dwelt in the fields of the suburbs of their cities, the lands allowed them out of the several tribes, where they lived when it was not the turn of their course to officiate at the temple; and to these, as to the priests in Jerusalem, a portion was distributed for the support of themselves and their families. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the same: for the priests in the field of the districts of their cities (compare Leviticus 25:34; Numbers 35:5), in each city, men were appointed — “expressed by name” (as at 2 Chronicles 28:15) — to give portions to every male among the priests and to all registered among the Levites.

Charles Ellicott renders it to the same effect: officers were likewise appointed to distribute portions to the priests and Levites who dwelt on their farms outside the sacerdotal cities, “men who were specified by names, to give portions to every male among the priests, and to every one that was registered among the Levites.” The “fields of the suburbs” he ties to Leviticus 25:34 and Numbers 35:5, the Levitical pasture-grounds, and notes the grammar — the relative omitted before the verb, which here stands in the perfect as at the eighteenth verse.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the reach of it as the crown of the whole administration: the priests in the country, who lived in the fields of the suburbs, were not overlooked in this distribution; those also had their share who were inhabitants of the villages, though they might be supposed to live at less expense. The preaching priests who stayed at home teaching the good knowledge of the Lord were maintained as well as the sacrificing priests who went up to Jerusalem, and those who abode by the stuff as well as those who warred the warfare. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the country priests on their allotted lands, Keil and Ellicott the named officers set to supply every male priest and registered Levite among them, Henry the fairness that forgot none. Together they show a provision that ran to the very edges of the land — down to the last priest on his pasture-farm and the last Levite in his village — so that the recovered wealth of the temple should reach not the favoured and the near only, but every servant of God in all the coasts of Judah.
20:
The long account of the reorganization closes with a verdict on the reformer: thus did Hezekiah throughout all Judah, and wrought that which was good and right and truth before the LORD his God. The reformed John Gill sums the deeds the words gather up — he settled the courses of the priests and Levites and made provision for them and their families. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the sentence as the conclusion of the whole matter: Hezekiah wrought in general that which was good and right and ha'emeth, the truth, before the Lord his God; and Charles Ellicott, of the same school, glosses that last word precisely — ha'emeth is “faithfulness, or sincerity.”

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unfolds the three terms into the portrait of a worthy king: “he is Good, and he does good; he is Upright, and he acts justly and maintains justice; he is truly Religious, and he lives according to that truth which he receives as a revelation from God.” The goodness, the justice, and the truth are not three praises loosely heaped but three faces of one integrity — the inner disposition, the outward conduct, and the governing revelation, answering one to another.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the general character of Hezekiah's services, and draws out its parts. His pious zeal reached to all the parts of his kingdom, “thus he did throughout all Judah,” and not the nearer regions only shared the good fruits of his government. He sincerely designed to please God, working that which was good before the Lord — “right,” that is agreeable to natural equity, and “truth,” agreeable to divine revelation and his covenant with God. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the concrete acts summed up, Keil the sentence as the account's conclusion, Ellicott the exact force of “truth” as faithfulness, Clarke the threefold portrait of the good, upright, and religious king, Henry the zeal that reached all Judah and the sincerity that aimed at God's approval. Together they set over the whole labour a single seal: that a king who had cleansed a temple, kept a Passover, purged the land of idols, and rebuilt the maintenance of a whole priesthood had done it all not for show nor for policy but “before the LORD his God,” good in heart, just in hand, and true to the revealed will he served.
21:
The chapter ends where a reformer's life is truly measured — not in the range of his works but in the heart he brought to them: in every work he began, in the service of the house of God, in the law and the commandments, to seek his God, he did it with all his heart, and prospered. The reformed John Gill enumerates the works the verse gathers: the cleansing of the temple, the providing of sacrifices, the placing of the priests and Levites in their order, and the care of their maintenance. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the words: “commandments” is properly the singular, commandment; “to seek his God” means “in order to seek,” or by way of seeking; and “he did it with all his heart” he sets beside the frequent phrase “with a perfect heart” (1 Chronicles 28:9) and the great command to love the LORD “with all thine heart” (Deuteronomy 6:5).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on that same clause and makes it the man's epitaph: “in every respect he was a thoroughly excellent man, saw his duty to God and to his people, and performed it with becoming zeal and diligence.” He turns it to a prayer: “may God ever send such kings to the nations of the world; and may the people who are blessed with such be duly obedient to them, and thankful to the God who sends them.”

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the two things the verse joins — wholeness of heart and prosperity of outcome. What Hezekiah began he went through with, prosecuting it with vigour and doing it with all his heart; and all his good intentions were brought to a good issue, for whatever he did in the service of the house of God and in the government of his kingdom, he prospered in it. Henry lifts it into a rule: “what is undertaken with a sincere regard to the glory of God will succeed to our own honour and comfort at last.” The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the several works, Ellicott the phrase “with all his heart” and its kinship with a perfect heart and the first great command, Clarke the excellency of the king and the prayer it draws, Henry the perseverance that finished what it began and the prospering that crowned it. Together they close the chapter on the secret of the whole reign: that Hezekiah's greatness lay not merely in cleansing, keeping, purging, and providing, but in doing every part of it “to seek his God” and with an undivided heart — and that such wholeheartedness, the witnesses agree, is what God prospered.
